title: Made in merica (2026 Remaster)
about:
Hello, as of Feb 5th '26! Yesterday, I had the hunch/feeling of wanting to listen to more of my old catalog again. I felt this time like going back to Made in merica, the first ever standalone project I made. It kind of seems to be of interest that the project is nearly about to turn 10 years old this year too. So not even intentionally, I am bringing new light to this old project all these years later, on the 10th anniversary essentially. I have been present all these years, and still it is amazing that this was 10 revolutions around the sun ago. I think I am now bound to think of life less about the number of years, and more about your presence to it. Not that I am not aging, I am. I think I was in 7th grade when I made this project. It was on my iPhone 5c, with GarageBand iOS 2.1. Live Loops were just added, and for whatever reason, I had always wanted to "make an album", so I thought I would try. That was the genesis to what started all of where I am at now. So I am very thankful that I got into it back then. It didn't get "fully original" until maybe 5 years later, with Elkosaurus Tex. At least I don't think I took the work seriously until that. I think Septem Numero was the first of my own "vision" if that makes sense though. But there's where you feel you started, and where you started. This is the start of it. There were demos before this, but some of them inevitably got deleted because I hadn't yet learned that I would want to look back on those later. Those were made before this project was created. It was a handful of them, probably from a spring break or summer break. I think this one took place over a few weeks, time gets confusing looking back. You remember it being different than it was, and thankfully project and file timestamps help out in that regard. Either way, it was just about 10 years ago.

I still have (most) of the project files for this album, being everything but tracks 6 and 7. I could maybe somehow recreate Googolplex as it was merely just with loops from the Live Loops grid. Drag Onward was more custom though. I made it like I did Bedlam and a few of the others. I would use the sample tracks from the GB library, and compose with those, as if you were to build out a track by choosing which stems you liked. I very much enjoyed this setup, albeit it wasn't very spontaneous, other than the song structure, and which loops you decided to use, when in the song, how it worked with other parts, things like that. There wasn't much room for unexpected curves, as I wasn't making the loops themselves. I've still wanted to go back and try out this way of writing, I haven't done it in a while. It hasn't felt natural/fun in a while. I now tend to improvise sections on top of one another, then mix it all from there. The changes in a song are dictated by how the previous stem was composed as I recorded it. So a song never is actually composed before it's played. I also don't know where it's going to go, because I don't plan out the first take. Maybe I have a vibe I want to write towards, or a goal for what vibe I want next on the album. But that is what dictates the direction, rather than "this song will sound like this". I think maybe that's why I enjoy funny tangents in albums too, because it's like I can tell which direction it "should/would" go towards, so I end up throwing a curveball and building off of that instead. That has been insurmountably fun and cool. I love doing that. Doing it too much does tend to remove the ability to connect with it if you don't get that aspect of it though. That might be why I relate Norm Macdonald's humor with my music. It's like I get the trajectory of where norms (no pun intended) tend to point towards, but then I do the opposite to point out that I am aware of which direction it "should" go, and instead do the opposite.

This album is very light on that, I hadn't quite gotten to that point yet. It was one of the few projects where it was supposed to be "good", plain and simple. The only rather explicit back reference humor is the title track. I think it kind of pokes fun at the album itself, in a positive light. That paves way for all of the meta-based writing I do now. This just shows it explicitly. I was curious about making a joke-related song on the album. The samples were created on my phone using dictation. I chopped them up into sounding like DJ samples or something like that.

Okay, but yeah, back to this release specifically. Loading the projects I *do* still have with modern GarageBand, they don't play correctly necessarily. I think either the samples have changed over time, or the rendering is different, or both. But the "sound" of the song is different now, because it's not using the same stems. Much like Septem Numero, I'd rather remaster the original lossy bounces rather than change the sound of the song itself, on accident. I have been looking into finding out how to maybe load an old version of GarageBand with old hardware, but I haven't been successful yet. That is the closest way to get the original master back. It still has the limiting issues, but at least it would sound identical, and would be lossless, to which I would then still remaster. In the event of that being a success, maybe I will look into this again. But for the time being, a remaster is okay. And also considering that tracks 6 and 7 (6-7???) are missing altogether, I wouldn't even be able to get lossless counterparts for those. But much like the 2013 remix for Sluggo!, some songs were still the original mixes, I think either because they liked those more, or because that's all that remained. I could do the same thing here too. But since it involves old hardware and software, right now it's not feasible as-is. If I find a way to get old GB running regardless, then I will absolutely probably look into it, at least to learn about the probability of whether it would help or not. This project just needs to sound better, and that's all, so even just a remaster is a neat way to do that!

Edit Feb 6,

Oh yeah, and for the source M4A files that this remaster (and the original release) are based off of, they were the original bounces from GarageBand iOS itself, and they were with the iTunes Plus setting if I remember right. When using `ffprobe` on the files, the bitrate seems to max out at about 270 kb/s, some being lower than that. Just some interesting info I thought I'd mention. The other pre-Flatlands albums which were also originally lossily-encoded were also using this same setting, so they also probably have comparable bitrates. And yeah, just to mention, Flatlands was the first project I bounced the masters as lossless. Looking back, it's kind of unfortunate, but it's okay. Have to learn somehow! Still debating whether I want to do a remix or remaster for Flatlands too, I really like that project. I still haven't even included it as the soundtrack for the game itself yet. Now I seem much more understanding of how to make that work, with all of my encoding knowledge now, with the likes of bitrates/sample rates, lossy and lossless, things like that. Back when I made the album, I was going to add it to the game through a hidden Bandcamp player. I think instead it would make a lot more sense to embed the album as high efficiency lossy encodes from the original sources, and bundle those with the game instead. That seems like a no-brainer now, but for some reason that didn't seem like the obvious option back then. Might do a remaster before doing that though. And I have a hunch that rendering Flatlands in Logic might present different sounds, much like the other projects I've tried to remix as of lately (this one, Septem Numero, etc). So I probably will have to go with a remaster too, unfortunately. Time will tell though.

I have the funny thought of making this into a vinyl release with Kunaki, since it would fit on a single side. Just an inclination. I would rather have something like Carpincho on vinyl though. This is an important release to me, but I don't think it's as monumental as some of the other works I've made. At least in regards to my own feeling towards them, and what they represent to me.

Edit Mar 1 '26:

What a crazy 24 hours. LCE source code leak, and MCPE v0.6.1?

That made me want to go back and listen to Volume Beta again, as that's around the time I was playing LCE I think, maybe 2015 to be more accurate. While listening to the first half of the album, multiple points of interest starting clicking in my ear. This album, and Ultimate Chaos, they are very much inspired from that time period, whether it was what my ear was listening to at the time (like whether it is a factor, which it is), as well as just what was very close to me as a musical experience. C418 and the Minecraft soundtrack were some of my first personal loves of music, which weren't rooted in the interests that others have showed me. It was part of my own personal experience, something I was fond of myself, 'unique to me' (I mean that in that it was something that I connected with on a personal level, memories attached; not to imply I am the only one affected by the music).

I think around this time was also when I started getting into Excision too, like things around Codename X, and Bass Cannon for example. Now it seems much more clear, these two facets very much emphasize my young mind at the time, and shows where my interests and fascinations were at, at the time.

It's very cool to look back with that context now, as usually you look back on the things you've done just as the things you've done, and you tend to forget or lose track of what inspirations led you to the point of wanting to do those things. Listening to pop at work (part of a coworker's playlist), it also reminded me how much that had an influence on me, even if it wasn't "my sound" in terms of what I relate and related to at the time. Things like LMFAO, Pitbull, a bunch of stuff I could probably name. I definitely was a 2010s kid, and looking back I am extremely fond of that "dubstep is just noise" kind of phase, where all people look at "the kids' music is crap" kind of thing. I also started watching asdfmovie this week, a new one dropped not too long ago! Side tangent, made a DVD of all the currently released episodes, for personal archival and memorabilia's sake. I want to make a GitHub repo to show how I did it, with yt-dlp, dvdauthor, and ffmpeg. Those tools are goated, love them with my life! But yeah. That's another facet to this album, which I seemingly forgot was a part of it. I don't know if I even had realized that it was that which was a part of this, either. Now it is obvious. That sly off-brand humor was from that 2010s YouTube-theme. And now it has morphed it's way into the Keneally and Zappa universe. I think that's why it was a bit confusing to understand Keneally and Zappa's humor, as I think I was trying to understand it from that asdfmovie/Vine "random"/"meta" humor point of view. It's more nuanced than that I think, less self-attacking as well. asdfmovie is chock full of that, and I love it. I think the Zappa/Keneally side of things isn't as blunt in the same vein. They are related, but different.

But yeah. So take Excision, Snarky Puppy, asdfmovie, and C418's Minecraft Volume Beta, and you end up with this project!

I should make a list of the references to things in this. I am listening to 'Kalifornia' for example, and I think it is kind of meant to sound similar to Big Ugly from Culcha Vulcha, which was also a big listen for me at the time.

Again, these are just GarageBand samples. But I think the cadence and song structures and production I was going for was somewhere along the lines of these influences. 'Made in merica' weirdness was the reference to asdfmovie, kind of. Maybe it wasn't LMFAO specifically, but whatever you might come to think of, as "generic 2010s pop" in the sense of mainstream popularity contest kind of pop. That's where I think 'Googolplex' and 'Made in merica' [title track] relate back to. And I think the title track was meant to poke fun at the structure of those songs. Use it's building blocks, but use the buildup in weird spots for example, and to jokingly make the song ridiculous. "Oh there's this crazy drop coming, oh man!" Then it happens, and it's this kind of silly wild synth that goes all over the place, but then it actually kind of slaps. Then the weird robot voice with odd lyrics, it's like tongue in cheek making the outro sick.

So I think this actually is my first album, even if I hadn't categorized it as such. It has my influence all over it, even if it was inspired from those names I mentioned. It's my experience and cross-breeding between these which is unique to me.

"And that's the end of my story :)"

Edit Mar 30 '26:

Just had some nice reconnections back to music I have liked over the years. You know those songs that influenced you, and you love and still love, but don't listen to regularly, and maybe aren't in your library? It's some of those. A lot of my very early inspirations from childhood I don't have in my library, not on purpose, but I think because I "know them so well", sometimes going back doesn't feel the same, and the memory is more strong than the future listens. Maybe that's not true, I don't know how to explain it though, so that's all I got. Like it's awesome when you hear the song randomly because it brings you back, but if you were to hear it in heavy rotation going forwards, it probably would lose it's luster that it once had for you. A lot of this seems to be singles for me as well, or rather parts of albums. Because my parents tended to buy only the songs they liked, I didn't necessarily always get the full album experience for an artist, which I thought for the longest time was a bummer. But now I am kind of intrigued in that I think the understanding of what I had made the artist to be in my head, that almost was a bigger picture than what it might be. I mean, like if a single sounds a certain way, maybe that's the outlier song. This definitely happens all the time, I mean my catalog has a lot of that too, where I try a style one-off, and the rest of my catalog sounds totally different.

But yeah. The songs that came to mind (first two) were when I was falling asleep last night. Rockwell Somebody's Watching Me and, Gorillaz Clint Eastwood. And thankfully my mind pulled together while I was trying to think of what other song Clint Eastwood reminded me of, and it worked out, and I remembered that it was RJD2 Ghostwriter. Man. I totally forgot how big that song was for me for probably a good 6 months or so. How that relates to this album? It's because it was right around or right before when I started on this album (the original release, not this remaster). It had always been in my dad's iTunes library, yet I think when going through his library to add music, I somehow had this fascination with this song, like I had known it a very long time. I don't know the extent to how much I had heard it before 'rediscovering' it back then, but it felt very nostalgic. And looking back now, it was before I understood anything about analog, digital, tape, vinyl, that sort of thing. But what I loved about the song was the analog sound, the crackle. So that was a bit jarring to realize when going back and listening today. It seems to obvious now. Very awesome. I think it definitely inspired seemingly this album, and maybe parts of Ultimate Chaos to some extent, not sure exactly how far it goes, I don't completely recall, I can just extrapolate looking back. So add that to the list of crossovers and inspirations, that's a big part of this project, and probably seemingly why I started to try making music.

There are a bunch of hyper-influencing songs for me, which I haven't documented either for myself or others, I want to do that sometime. Plenty of 'random' things. Another that I came across, I think because I heard it at work (that's been the source for a lot of reencounters lately) was Paper Tongues Road to California, and 1901 on Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix. There are multiple other songs on that album too, I think. It was when I was too young to really discern lyrics, and I very much just understood the 'sound' of the music. It's almost like I only heard lyrics as an instrument, the melody was more keen to my ear than the words. That seemingly is still why I struggle with more lyrical-driven music, I have the goal to get better at my lyrical-ear, it's already gotten better over the last few years. I am now starting to notice that maybe it's a mix thing for me. If the instruments are on equal plane with the vocals, I am probably going to listen to the instruments. So when I have lyrics in my songs, I want them to be at the forefront. Not to say that I don't like the sound of the mixed songs that the vocals sit in on, I actually love it. I just haven't had the ear to discern the words themselves yet. Like I love the sound of 1901. And I am glad that I have the discerning part to know 'indie' now. I just only knew the 'sound' from that it was on the radio, on 91X. There was a little CD player my dad gave me in my room, it had FM and AM on it. I haven't been much of a radio guy in practice, but that was my starting ground, I think because it's how we listened to music together when in the car. It's like when XM took off too (or rather, at home we started using it; in the car I mean). So I'd say pre-2010s it was a more radio-based listening experience for me. Much of my seemingly indie background came from that. I didn't know it was that, I didn't hear the lyrics, and I seemingly was just building my 'music knowledge' from it. I am only prefacing it like that because I don't think I did get the entire scope of it from those years. If you are just getting into building your musical ear, you can't really catch everything. So that's what I'm intrigued by. Like I didn't know much about the bands, nor the names, I didn't know the artwork, I just knew the sound of it. Same with the word parts. Like even back when I was super little, another very influential song (again, among a huge bunch) was System of a Down Hypnotize. I always called it "The Ding Song", now looking back, it was the cymbal bell (and maybe a small percussive thing too). My dad had mentioned multiple times that he hadn't even heard that part before, so he was always perplexed by why I called it that. Examples of that are very interesting now, it seems to line up with my ear for things like mixing now, where certain elements are what I pick up on. So maybe that's compositional as well, not sure. I am very happy my dad showed me a bunch of different music styles, much of that is thanks to him, and I did a lot of things building off of that original foundation. Oh yeah, Lisztomania for sure as well.

But yeah, so many songs we just had on shuffle in the car, I think it was his iPod classic, which he gave me maybe 6 months ago, as he hasn't used it for years. I think all of this is why I haven't ever moved over to streaming, nor to subscriptions. This self-curated and interest-based listening style has been present since the beginning, and it's not new for me. I am once again, very thankful for that too, because I hear a lot of people mention that they wish they hadn't gotten rid of their CDs from the past, things like that. But I never had to experience that loss, because it was always there.

Another one was Beck. I always have loved his songs. I only heard a few here and there, because that's all that was in our library. So namely, Jackass, Devil's Haircut, ones like that. Probably all of the hits. So while I didn't get the full perspective of all those artists back then, it seemingly did give a wide picture of different sounds, which I only just currently actively right now see is probably a benefit. I could see how radio and or maybe maybe streaming would help with this. So different listening styles probably lead to different results as well, namely what genres you write, what styles you mix, things like that. I think I have kind of settled into a certain sound as of lately, but what sound it is, is always changing, because I try to not stay with the same songs for a long time. I have been trying to onboard multiple albums every few months. Been doing that since probably 2022 or earlier, in the grand scheme of things. Always searching, connecting dots, finding collaborations, or previous works not yet popularized. Like I got into Opeth in 2022 because I learned that Steven helped with production on Blackwater Park, and Damnation. And when going through more of the Wikipedia article, I found Storm Corrosion. I found that because of the connections. So this technique, albeit newer for me in the relative scheme of things, it has been very successful. Same with listening to artists that my favorite artists like. I got Ryuichi Sakamoto's album Heartbeat because I know Marco Minnemann loves his work. Man, a great album. And as of recently, been trying to get into albums because of "what they speak to me", whether it's what I can gather from the name of the artist, album, track names, or write up. At a music store in La Mesa, there was a dual-CD project called Pigface that I was intrigued by, and have yet to check out. I already did some buying that day though, so I didn't get any albums that time. There was also a prog-looking album that kind of looked like the video for P.T./C.C. Harridan, and an experimental album with Mandelbrot sets all over it, and the names were very funny too. I probably will go back and get all of these, maybe. We'll see. It has to be an in-the-moment connection or understand, I feel like. If I am open to what the CD looks like it might sound like, then I should get it. Asking my dad about this, he hasn't ever done this. "Why would I spend 3 bucks on an album I might not know I will like?". He has a point. I think this is a new thing that is an interest of mine, as I hadn't operated like this in the past either. It feels to freeing, it's amazing. I very much more enjoy used things now, as of the last year or two.

Long story, but yeah. It's amazing how big your early inspirations and experiences are for your life! I can't wait to be a role model like my parents are for me. And working on integrating with my emotions has been a great thing the last month or two. I think this process started a bit ago, but I wasn't aware of what was missing until as of recently.

title: Bugabot Camelot
about:
[Jan 19 '26]
Just started this thing today. Pulled together a bunch of the names I had written down from the last few months.

This song was very improv-based, in the spirit of fun playing, more than anything else. I think my playing has been very solo-focused as of lately, probably because of having just bought Ziltoid lately, and listening to my old work again, from around the Scary House days. Realized that I haven't had as much improv in terms of writing. It usually starts with a vision, then I make a song "mathematically" around it. That has it's merit, and I love writing like that. I do miss some of these jam sessions though. This harks back to that, in spirit.

With practicing 3 note per string a bunch for some reason, that seems to be the playing style inspiration from this. It is on my Orville, in standard tuning.

I took mixing queues from The Who, Tommy. Love the stereo usage, trying that out again, but with that as a reference. Took some mixing and mastering queues from the Robot Dog Studio channel.

Oh yeah and I think the improv-based playing is inspired by listening to Keneally a ton as of recently, both because I am more into it very much again, but also because I will be going to see him up at The Baked Potato on Wednesday.

This song [Psychosis] was the first time I bounced all of the tracks as stems, then mixed from there, rather than mixing from the takes themselves (configurable DAW plugins; now they are baked in, I have to use mixing to make it work on it's own instead, rather than going back and adjusting the literal tones).

It's a Logic Pro bass amp sim, Neural Amp Modeler for the Mesa-like sound, and another tone with NAM for the clean one. Just Logic drums too, tapped out on my iPad with Logic Remote connected to my Mac with USB-C for ultra-low latency. It very much helps with the MIDI not breaking when I do blast beats.

The artwork wasn't intended to look insanely similar to Scambot 1 [but it does], sorry about that. It seems like it just does though, so yeah, it's a bit on the nose in terms of reference. But that's okay. The music kind of is as well, so aah. haha

Using two stages of compression for guitar takes is killer, don't be afraid of it! I actually don't mind the mix here. It was hackily done, but I used my ear, and I think it's actually fairly clear, while a bit quirky.

I tried using Voxengo for the Mid-Side field, but it didn't sound nice for this specific panning, so I didn't use it here. Was also going to use Sketch Cassette, but it didn't seem like it needed it.

The title of [Psychosis] is about how everyone nowadays is in psychosis because of social media. Because apps use webviews to render their pages, rather than being an actual app (inconsequential, just a funny observation), people are just using the Internet, but through a dumbed-down filter, where the site picks what you search for. So rather than using the Internet where you get to pick where your interest goes, instead you have the site do it for you. And the "app" part of it is made to seem like it's personal to you. Idk. Just making up reasons as to how I came up with that name. Some names I come up with in bed just as I am falling asleep, then I get up probably 10 times as I come up with a different bunch of names and have to go write them down. So they don't necessarily make sense to describe after the fact, it's like the remnants of your thoughts in your mind are circling down the sleepy drain, and you are writing them down as they clear out. Yeah.

So this may turn into a project, we'll see. I like the improv side of things again, and trying out more mixing experiments could be fun with it. Open-ended again. It just feels natural. This is fun right now, that solo-based 3 note per string soloing band kind of sound. I haven't done too too much of it since having moved to Logic, so it is kind of a curiosity as to how it might sound with a good mix and master. :)

Today is the 1/19 by the way, as this probably will be a long-running project :)

edit: A few minutes later, after publishing this :)
I think my playing/recording [in the past] was more driven around what was fun to hear when I was playing, rather than being inspired by what I was listening to. Maybe in some way or another it was inspired by it, but it was very feel-driven before. Like nowadays maybe I would get inspired by a sound, then use that to create the song, in terms of what it was started from. But early on, it was that I would record by ear, like if I were to play a band as myself. Then this is what would get tracked in as a specific song. That's what this is trying out with again. I think I kind of forgot about this kind of writing I used to do. I think my current listening habits might have been inspired by it too, so it kind of goes both ways. So rather than letting the instrument lead the song where it goes, I have been having an inspiration from something in the world, and write around that thing. So maybe it's more emotion-based than I had realized? Maybe just not with words as much. Like when I used to "mess around" on guitar back when, I would have one track that I came up with, then I would listen back and see what else I could come up with for that. It still does that with the inspired-writing, but it has to cater to the aesthetic it's trying to convey or explain. This instead is more about the flow of what the instrument is trying to play.

And by solo-based writing, I mean that in the compositional-sense. The way I am playing the guitar is less about riffs in the genre sense, and more about the building-block sense. It's up to much more interplay, ear-based listening, fun little calls back and forth. So recording a guitar idea, this is more akin to that, than making a song on it's own, at least I feel. The starting clean track for this song is more like what ideas I would record with Music Memos than what I would make a song with now. Again, not good or bad, just great to learn what I use and have used as song structures over time. My early guitar albums were very much driven by this solo-based writing. I miss it! And yeah, I think I forgot how to do it. It does make it to where the work can't have as much of a clear vision though, and maybe that's why I may have moved away from it for some time, to learn how to make music around the vision; even if I didn't know what the vision might be, per se. I get a feeling of where the arrow points, and I follow that. For this, there is no arrow, only vibe. It's like sitting in a hot tub, vs reading a history book. This is the hot tub. And it's fucking bubbly as fuck. Fuck.

Oh yeah. And [Psychosis] wasn't recorded to a click, intentionally. I haven't done that in a while, and that is an aspect to the demo nature of things that was present back then too. Because it was composed as just a demo, that's how it was presented too, at least in terms of how counterparts intermingled and things like that. Note that it's never meant to be demo quality, that's part of why I got so bummed with how my music sounded in 2023. It's supposed to be kind of like a demo in terms of inspiration/improv, but not quality. I like the rawness of first takes, but I want the production quality of albums. That's what I have been aiming for for a long time.

If this song were to be more like something from Tommy, it definitely needs vocals. I do want to look into making vocal songs. Maybe I can find a way to get vocal-based writing onto this project. I think it would probably allow for it somehow. Not sure where it would fit into the writing stage though. A song like this for example, would be too busy with vocals in it. It's already a bit busy, just right on the line I think. If I had turned on Low Latency Monitoring, it would have helped the first 7 minutes of the song. That's okay, now remembered for next time. It's more crucial even more so when the metronome is off.

Edit Jan 20:

Okay, new concept. I didn't like the mix of the first song. So I tried making a second mix. Learned how much I actually really like the sound of mono drums. New realization. The gain staging and master compression is a bit better in my opinion too, the first take was a bit too quiet and inconsistent. I think it was because I was in tutorial hell a bit too much, and wasn't as creative with it. So these are the same stems for Mix 2, but a stronger gain mix, and a different stereo field. I also was interested again today about a classic recording sound, so I tried that out. This one was inspired by some Ozzy that was on at work. I seemingly like the cut highs on the recording, so I tried that with Linear Phase EQ on the master. Mono drums, relatively hard panned guitars, but with Voxengo to fill out the Mid-Side channel. Makes hard panned sound great in my opinion. Feels very filled-out. And ChromaGlow with Sketch Cassette really makes it sound crushed. That combined with the lower highs, it does sound like a classic recording I feel. I don't know if it's necessarily a great sound yet, not "clear", but I wasn't really going for that either. So maybe that's what this project is, idk. Maybe I will try mixing the same song in different ways and see what happens. That could be fun. So far I like Mix 2 the best I think. Just fixed some of the issues from earlier.

Was going to use room reverb, but I didn't want it to get lost in the crush noise of the master production. Maybe Mix 3 will have that clean sound I like, and or with room reverb. Many iterations at hand here. Maybe this can just be a "fun" project, rather than a statement or something. It's a statement about learning I guess. Experiment, and don't worry about it! Lots to learn about here. May be neat for me to pick up on different things I like to do in terms of production, too.

Edit Jan 23:
Last night, I was seemingly inspired by the concept of "composing", in the literal sense. Rather than just "creating" or improving, I was curious about the concept of arrangement, and stacking parts which complement each other. I think I have sort of utilized this in the past, this time it was more intentional I think. I wanted each part to have a purpose. Not shure (typo, kind of a funny pun lol) how these songs relate to each other in style yet, but now I am starting to like what this project has going for it. Excited to see what other things I try moving forward. I think getting "The Universe Will Provide + Parallel Universe" from the Keneally show up at The Baked Potato, and with watching DTP "Higher" again, and watching his podcast about how progress for The Moth was going, and how he had to write out all of the queues for the in-ear for each of the band members (orchestra included), for whatever reason this kind of stuck in my brain. I'm not one (yet, maybe?) to listen to exclusively orchestral music, I think maybe my ear is a little more receiving to understanding arrangement and things like that now though, and I think the MKBFD show exemplified that, too. Realizing that I was interested in the way each of the players complemented each other, and it is in a rock setting, I love and loved that. That's what I love about The Aristocrats too.

So yeah, with all of that in mind, I kind of turned my "interest" brain and "logic" brain off, and just tried to create a piece where each part was meant to work with the part next to it. I made these songs, tracks 2/3/4 on my phone, just in bed lol. I even tried out to "hackily" mix the tracks in GarageBand *only*, using my new fangled knowledge of EQ curves and compression per track. Wow, that, along with proper gain staging headroom (turn everything down BEFORE you start mixing!), it seems much much better in terms of clarity. I think the clarity of my Logic mixes may still be a little better. But that being said, I did it just with my phone speakers, no headphones even. I don't know the EQ reference curve of my iPhone speakers, so I just went with it. I am fairly familiar with how things sound on there though, so maybe that helped it a bit too, it's not a totally blind mix. I didn't have any gain meters, loudness meters, or things like that though, since GB iOS is very limited in that way. So it was a great exercise to see if I could use my ear with the limited tooling that was available, very pleased with. Bounced those to lossless files, then mastered them in GB iOS as well. Again, blind, since there's barely any meters or a mixing pane. But light compression followed by some light EQ, it seemed to really work well. GB iOS only bounces at 44.1/24, so I opened it in Logic on my Mac to merely raise the loudness with my LUFS meter in hand, and a limiter. Then I bounced that with POWr #2, at 44.1/16. So there was only that second stage of mastering, merely for loudness adjustment and limiting of unexpected peaks which GB iOS doesn't clip.

Very happy with the results, considering it was mostly by ear.

So again, this does prove, both in general and to myself, it's not necessarily the tools, it's how you use them, or rather, whether you know how to utilize them effectively. In other words, I did not know how to before haha.

I think the biggest thing here might actually be the carving EQ for each of the pieces in the arrangement, it really does wonders. Leave room for bass guitar, leave room for strings, leave room for drums, and if anything, bring the drums down a little to where it leaves room for other things. So reverse to what I believed a few years ago, less volume and less EQ is the answer, not more. You cut room for each instrument, rather than raise each one on top of the other. It's like a puzzle, but to where you cut out the divots, rather than cut the notches off, and tape them onto edges that didn't have them. Uh, yeah.

A great example is Bugabot Camelot, I think it actually sounds great, even if the song compositionally "sucks". I like it, that's besides the point. Maybe it's more an exercise than anything. I find I can't play MIDI guitar, bass, or strings very well at all, so maybe that's why it sounds like that. MIDI keyboard works nicely though, as you can hear from tracks 2/3.

I also am not a fan of quantization. I'd rather hear the little hiccups, I really don't care about them at this point. If you can play relatively in time, your brain can hear what you were attempting to do. It sounds more realistic too, even if it's with not as high tech MIDI sounds. I honestly kind of like the unique sound of it, in a familiar kind of way. Like it sounds pedestrian or something.

I also realized this week while going back through some of my older work that I did tend to over-EQ things, so I tried to use more cutting, and less raising in general. Like if I wanted to raise the treble of the guitar for example, only raise it at most like 1db, rather than 2 or 4. Some of my older mixes feel a bit sharp, like they are pointy. Very bassy, and very trebley. So that is another thing I am experimenting with, albeit not cognizant of it. Rather than trying to EQ the shit out of the master, just make sure the faders sound correct to begin with, and that the EQ of each track is leaving room for one another. Then when mastering, it's more about compression, light EQ to brighten everything a little (and cut the mud, aka 150-300 range), then a limiter and loudness check to make sure the playback is at a nice consistent volume from track to track. And yes, compression doesn't need to be insane, I personally am setting my loudness to around 12 LUFS. I can't quite decide whether to use higher LUFS. Some say they go around 9, I guess it just depends which you like. May do some experimenting in that regard. I also like the idea of having track to track LUFS changes, seems like a nice composition tool too, dynamics in the album sense, since the album is a cohesive work, in concept, too.

I also used some light automation for parts which were a little too loud throughout the song, on track 3 (Sofa). It was kind of inspiring to use it more as a mixing tool, rather than a creative sound. I think that's been one of the biggest changes to learn over getting into mixing and mastering. It's that you are making the sound of it more defined, rather than doing creative changes to the message it's conveying. Back on early projects like Made in merica, I used automation, but as a compositional creative aspect to the writing process. It wasn't about the mixing part of it. So now it makes a lot more sense, you just write the song as is, then use automation to emphasize certain parts where they should shine, as you understand them to need to be. This is much different, and I love it. Just a different mindset to be in.

So this project is very much open-ended so far, where I am aiming for high-quality, not perfection though. Hitting the target isn't the point, it's that I aimed for it, and I am getting closer to "the bullseye". The point is that writing, composing, mixing, all of it, it's a moving target too, though. I like that though. Like many other things, it ends up spiraling into something more that you had no idea about. Programming was like that too. I got into it for web dev, frontend specifically. I now write Rust projects, who knew?

And I am bouncing to 44.1/16 because for me at least, I don't see that as not being a logical target. I know some streaming platforms allow for higher sources, but I am not one personally to discern how it is better in terms of a listening or distribution medium. It's one thing to record with high bitrates and sample rates, I do believe in that, and I do do that. The processing leaves more room for various concepts, which others have explained much better than I (Monty Montgomery, check out the videos he's made on YouTube). So until I am perceptive to the benefits of a listening experience higher than CD quality, I will release at CD quality. Archival and captures of things like vinyl, again I understand why you would want to capture as much detail as possible. In terms of the delivery format and what listeners listen with, CD quality seems to be the sweet spot. As I've mentioned, I use dithering when going from 24 to 16 bit as well, even if it doesn't "make a difference". I'd rather use it than not. And since I like to make CDs of my work anyways, I would rather not have it so that digital copies are of differing quality to physical releases. If you own the CD, you should have the best quality, the same as everything else. That would be annoying if you wanted the physical copy, but the Bandcamp version had more quality. I wouldn't buy both, would you? It's just more of a headache. Those are just my opinions though, which I have gathered over the past year or so.

And as to why my older releases fluctuate in sample rate and bitrate? I didn't know any better, and I had "understood" that "higher quality is better". So yeah, not much reasoning, I just didn't know enough about it, so I just bounced the best that I could. Mind you, with less than clear mixes as well. So it's not like you are benefitting from that high quality.

GarageBand iOS only seems to bounce at 44.1/24 anyways, so it's not like 48khz is always an option. It used to bounce at 48/24, but that seemed to have been an accident or something? I think it was always labeled as 44.1/24, but it was upsampling it by default, eek. Glad they changed it at least. And recording audio tracks in GB iOS seems to only be at 44.1 too, so at some point you'd have to upscale things at some point anyways.

When doing projects in Logic Pro exclusively though, I always use 48/24. Then I master those sources, and bounce to 44.1/16 with dither, for the final masters. Ideally one would probably bounce it all at 48/24, then dither separately, but I am not on the side of having wanted to do that yet. Again, once I have a reason to learn to do otherwise, then that is different. Just like how I bounced at "the highest quality available" because it was "best". I don't know why I would currently need 48/24 masters, if anything I can still go and bounce it from the mastering project too, since everything was already rendered from the mix tracks anyways (no worries about external plugin changes). Of course I guess unless Voxengo Mid-Side were to change or something, then eegh. 

Everything comes in small increments. I will probably bounce as both down the road, when a project permits as such. I am just happy with the mixes now, so much better than the past. "You can't build Rome in a day"!

Oh yeah, and I haven't listened to the Universe CDs yet, just the thought of how the arrangement for those, as well as his band, that was the inspiration for things.

Edit Jan 27 '26:

Okay, this project is complete. It's not that I felt that it concluded, but more that the next wave of things seemed to launch off from where this one was going. "Recreational Outrage 2", yes. That's all I have to say for the time being. Similar in roots, possibly a little different in articulation.

tracksInfo.title: Woodsmell
tracksInfo.about:
Just recorded this today (Jan 26 2:43 PM as of writing). Been listening to some of my older work, which I think I have mention again. Wow. Really had a lot of great things going back then. Not from a third person [ego] perspective, I am merely saying in that I realize how strong my vision was for what I was dreaming to create, and I think merely my knowhow was the thing holding the work back from being what it could be.

This song today was recorded on my iPhone with GarageBand iOS. I used my iRig 2, a Lightning 3.5 mm adapter, [iPhone 12 mini], and earbuds for monitoring. This is how I recorded the first few guitar albums back then. I thought it would carry forward similarly in creative intuition to the other installments from this project thus far. So it's very much rooted in that original creative drive that I seemingly have had a tough time to rediscover. It's okay that that's the case, and I can't explain enough how great it has been to remember what it was exactly that was present when recording those, and why I may have lost sight of it over time. I could probably go make a podcast about this, and I probably will. As a pre-empasis explainer, the creation of it is where the golden ticket has to be located. That comes first. It's not something you can build, learn, or whatever other actionable thing you can do to "get it". If you *want* to make a song, a song will come out. If you want to *have* a song, it will sound like absolute trash. Or at least your feeling and sentiment to it will be as such.

This state of mind I am rekindling, it's that open-ended inspiration, where you are just experimenting, having fun, and just making do with what is. There has to be a lot at play for that mindset to be present, and healthy. Maybe it has to do with mental health, or merely listening to your mind and body. Whatever the "magic potion" is, that seems to be the case for me at least. I need sleep, food, no stress, or emotional strife. I very much am understanding again how this all connects together. Where you are coming from when you sit down to write, that's the entire thing. So if you are coming at it from an angle that isn't going to help you, don't expect positive results, I mean in the way that you discern how you did.

Okay, yeah. So this was with my Orville, using only GarageBand drums (SoCal I think?), and the built-in amp sims. I used my 5 string SDGR bass (the one I use for all my own bass tracks; there's only the one bass :) ), again built-in amp sim.

I only used earbuds for the monitoring process. I did all of the mixing with merely my phone speakers. The goal is and has been (for tracks on this project which apply) to again start looking into the limitations of what you can do with what you have. This is how I learned so much about what I do now. I love that mechanism for learning. I specifically didn't use the earbuds because the EQ and just general audio presence is horrible. I got them at Target for like $10, I just needed them for the plane ride to SquiggleConf, and I wanted to get familiar (in my more recent role as an audio engineer/mindset) with low-quality hardware listening. I need to know what different "distribution targets" sound like. It's like how you view your frontend at different browser/screen sizes. You want to know how a mix will carry across different systems.

Yeah. So I did the mix on my phone speakers, landscape (stereo speakers). The goal as I think I've mentioned has been to really work on a solid mix, as that goes the longest way. That seems to have helped dramatically. Gain stage much below full scale. Pan instruments to fill out the stereo field. Ensure volume sounds okay where each instrument pokes out just right enough so you can hear each one. Where each instrument overlaps in frequency range, cut EQ paths for each one to leave room for which one you want in front. Think of this like z-index for CSS, where you might be lowering the opacity a bit of certain elements too. Maybe you want the edge of a card to show through to what's behind it. Or you could use clip-path. You just don't want the background to fully fall away, or the two to create an incoherently blurred or colored blob. That's what EQing does to leave room for each part.

Okay, then I bounced all of that into a 44.1/24 file (using GB iOS for the bounce). I then mastered it in a new project. I did some automation to make the start and end of the track a little more easy on the ears (sound-stage speaking), and applied compression and EQ as necessary to make the final file sound more cohesive (opinionated, weighted into what you feel is more sonically pleasing to your ears/what your vision of how the song should sound is). Then I bounced that master to another 44.1/24 file.

I then opened it one more time with Logic on my Mac. I was planning on only doing loudness management (LUFS checking), where I add a limiter to manage peaks, and raise the gain to make the LUFS more streamlined with the other songs on the project.

I then felt when listening on my Mac speakers (again, trying to low-budget see how/whether I can get things done without a lot of gear) that the track needed one more layer of compression (felt too dynamic, hard to hear quiet parts, loud parts too jarring), and the EQ could use a bit trimming of the low-end and high-end (and a little bit more mud cleanup). So I use Linear Phase EQ for that.

The stack for it was a Vintage VCA (tried that, and somehow felt giddy when listening to how great it made it sound. Not sure why it felt and different, just went with that emotional response to the sound of it. So, I don't know why it's better quite yet, but I responded to it, so I am taking that instinct as a learning moment; progress, instincts trusted over logic!!), and the default settings were great, I just adjusted it slightly to whatever "felt" right (weighted, hard to explain). Then it was the Linear EQ (helps prevent phase issues on the master), and finally the Limiter with the gain increases (up to 12 LUFS average).

I then felt the stereo field felt a bit shallow, or rather that the center felt a bit empty. I now started to get another another understanding for mastering, in the concept of working on the stereo field. I placed a Voxengo Sound Delay on the Mid-Side route, and tried a few different delays. Setting the x0.01 setting to 4 sounded magical for some reason. Again, flipping back and forth, I can hear how it adds the center, I just don't quite get why it made it so neat sounding. I tried turning it on and off, and with the Mid-Side present it definitely sounded much more full, the panning was much more cohesive. Then I would solo the 'mid channel' (not a real channel, just a perceptive one, very intriguing), and it really does just sound like a mono mixdown of the entire mix. So I think that's what's placed in the center of it.

The drums are still stereo, I'm not sure how I can make them mono in GB iOS. Maybe I could do a Merge Tracks action of some sort? I think that usually keeps it stereo though.

But yeah, Voxengo was just before the Limiter. I then made sure one more time it was set to 12 LUFS, then that was that! Bounced at 44.1/16 with POWr #2 dithering, and called it a day! Now it's 3:11 PM, and I am going to finish the edit for this.

The takeaway from today: The vision was never the thing to fix, it's to put focus on how you articulate the vision, and to make that stronger. Learning, experimenting, practicing, and making your own conclusions and opinions about how you work, that's how you are then able to make your vision into reality.

Keep creating friends! It's really fun.

Love ya.
Brandon

P.S.

As I was finishing the bass track, near the end of the song my posture wasn't too nice, just getting cozy while playing. My head was resting on the wood of the bass, and my nose kind of smelt it a little. Hence, the title. The peculiarity again was what made it stuck.

And for this track, things were recorded much like Gridelda the Snitch. Have been wanting to try that out again for some time now. It's that a singular improvisation is the root of the source for the track, but when recording the other parts, you *only* listen to that one when recording the other parts on top. I think what I like about it is that your mind isn't trying to write around the other parts, and they end up working together, but in their own worlds. It almost makes it sound like multiple people are playing, rather than it all being one written part. So I only ever heard my current instrument, and the drums, when tracking. Then I mixed it from there, hearing all the parts together. I actually haven't even heard the song all the way through being finalized, yet. That's also kind of interesting about my projects too, in that I sometimes don't even do a full listen before I release it. So it's just as much of a discovery to me as it is to you. Really neat.

Yeah, Lordsmith, Transcend, and Scary House have been in rotation as of recently. Really like and liked what energy was going on during that time, and I think I am finding it again, as I mentioned probably 20 minutes ago, just above.

And another thing, it probably explains why things get so far out of time with one another. If one track has delay, and I play that, it introduces that into the monitoring when recording the next track, and the next one. And the next one. Say I record the drums. Not much delay. I record guitar with that as a reference. Probably a little bit of delay. I then record another guitar part. My mind might start listening to the first guitar part for ear reference. But then that makes it 2x delayed. So now it's way off from the drums. Then I go to record bass guitar, and the beats and transients and too hard to discern to improvise with, so then you get frustrated and start making a bunch of weird noises because you are annoyed. Then you get annoyed that you messed up your song. You lose train of thought, and the song idea is lost to time. Then you go to mix the song, and the recording frustrates you, because it's so out of time. And since the song was improvised, that's the only take. So there's no reference to what you were thinking back then, so you can't really go back and re-record it, as the idea is gone. Then all of that internalizes itself into being "what kind of musician you are", or "what kind of music you play", or "do you play music? Yeah I try". Lack of confidence. Not thinking what you make is real. And it was all because of monitoring delay. Man. That sucks. And maybe all of that was present to begin with, and it merely brought it to the surface. Maybe low self-esteem was a problem regardless of whether your DAW has low latency. Maybe the mix sucks because you didn't yet have the ear training to discern or understand what makes good mixes good. And why would you expect yourself to have had that training, when you hadn't trained for it? So with all of that in mind, stop being so fucking god damn hard on yourself, it's okay man! You're killing it, and maybe just find out when, why, and how things aren't working out how you'd like, then reconfigure your goals around that. That's actionable.

[I; me] Love it. This is awesome. Music has taught me so much.

And don't worry about hiding those "mistakes" along the way. Because showing all of that progress only helps you see how much you've grown, and it provides a reference point to others to teach them how you got to where you are at, and it can help them see what things may be helpful to arriving at their vision, too. Not everyone has the same vision. That's beautifully baffling too. Not that I would expect everyone to. Just, in that, take a moment and think about that. Isn't that amazing? There's so many different goals and things people want from life.

Life is fucking beautiful, unc.
❤️

title: Glide
about:
Hello from the late night of Sept 28, '26. This was originally merely just the single 'Glide'. I had two other tracks from these sessions which I very much loved, I think I just emotionally hadn't metabolized them to the extent of being able to publish them. I love them a lot.

This was one of the most difficult times of my life, during this period. I can talk more about it later, if I haven't already described it. I think it's still a bit raw to talk about, and I want to let it have it's time. This album is representative of peace and moving forwards, in the face of hardship. Life chooses what path we go down. Even if we choose which paths to take. Acceptance of that 'fate' is how we find peace. That sounds very deep. This was a very deep album though, and during a very growth-focused point of my life.

In retrospect, Half Awake sounds a lot like this project. I actually much prefer my mixing/mastering in this project, to that of Half Awake. So between the two, this may have better production. Maybe I can go back and do a remix/remaster of Half Awake, later on.

After having been listening to Ki a lot recently, this album actually sounds a lot like Ki, interestingly enough. And, in retrospect once again, it's interesting how this album seemingly played a similar role in my life to that of what Ki did for Devin. I think it's ultimately that 'surrender' kind of thing, from what I can describe from my [limited] personal experience/perspective. I am pretty sure I used some sort of open tuning here too, probably something resemblant to that of Open C, but it was more improv-tuned than that. So some of the open notes I play here even remind me of Ki, I think it was Winter, which I was listening to today actually. Very very cool. I definitely hadn't even listened to Ki yet by the time I made this. I had indeed been listening to a whole ton of Ghost though, so that's probably the common ancestor here. The sound of this slice of my catalog feels like it borrows from Night Verses I feel, too.

The project folder for this album included "Can't Quite Quantify" as well. That purely doesn't fit with this album in sound or genre though, so it will stay as it's own single.

This was also one of those projects where it wasn't trying to be a specific sound, it just was. And it was such a release for me, emotionally, like a release of emotions. It still took a long time after for things to metabolize, and I think I am feeling better about things later in the year now. There are new challenges, but man has changing course and making the best strides I can, really worked and really helped. Hope is the way forwards.

Love, and goodnight.
- Brandon ❤️

Oh yeah, and I think the tracks 'named themselves' after having recorded them, if I recall correctly. Track 2 is something specific, the other two seemingly are more subconscious in nature. Dendron was just the cool word that came into my head, again if I remember right. But man, that is such a great description for how I was feeling. It's like we, as life, as family, as humans, in relationships, in life, what have you, it feels like we are all a tree, in the sunset. And I had just lost a very important leaf which I looked up to. All of us leaves have limited time here. That's what this one is about.

Edit Oct 3: Okay, I had called this Glide when the first song got published. I still like the title "Beautiful Days" when I had made this into an album. But, in retrospect, the title track is still the epitome of the whole thing. So I am going to make the 'album' titled Glide once again, instead of "Beautiful Days". Edit, while having just written that. Actually, no, I'm gonna keep it as that. This is dedicated to someone near and dear to my heart.

While listening through this project, after Glide, at least for The Peach, I feel like *take it or leave it* the second two songs could be 'bonus' tracks. While I am not going to mark them as such, I feel they are. The main presence of this release is Glide. That one is 100% the feeling and vibe. The Peach is great, I think it is very long to be fair though. But again, the sense of sitting with the feelings and just going through them, that's part of the sentiment too. So that's why I think it is part of the intent of this project. It is what it 'is', in a sense. In terms of listening experience, I think 'Glide' is just enough to 'get' it though. Maybe I will come back and change my mind on this. Either way, yeah. Up to you for how you feel.

Edit maybe 20 minutes later:

Okay, ended up going back to "Glide" as the title. I like the other two songs, and their emotional home, in where they come from. But to me, the main drive of this release is undoubtedly "Glide". The other two songs are "finished", to the best of what they can be. But I don't 'like them', to the extent that I LOVE "Glide". So, yeah. I am still releasing/including them because they are cool, and they are great to share. They are great context for the writing I was doing at the time too. I love context. I still love the title "Beautiful Days", I am reserving it for the important reference that this time period is rooted from though. This release is called "Glide", like the song.

tracksInfo.title: Glide
tracksInfo.about:
[from YouTube]
We are lucky to be here. Remember the soil under your feet. Remember to stop and look at that view. Remember to tell your loved ones you love them. Do not take your time here for granted.
[ok back to the original description]

Okay, might be working on a new album, not totally sure. Just making what I am making, and then seeing where it goes. I'm not one usually for singles. But I am too eager to release these, they make me too happy with how they sound. So maybe they will eventually be compiled into a project after the fact. These are the only two songs I have made so far. It's not that I am releasing them out of a selection of songs I don't like. It's just that they feel like they need to be made public right now. I'm just following that intuition. I don't know how they fit together. I just know that they are what I need to be making.

This one was a guitar improvisation with my Orville Les Paul. Used some new plugins, and the new mixing/mastering techniques I mentioned in the previous song.

The song felt like it was to be called Glide. It was going to have a paper airplane on the cover, but I felt like an "improvised" cover might make more sense for the art. Just been feeling that lately. The artwork kind of brought my mind into feel like it's a place or time you "aren't meant to reach". Not in a negative light, but more in that you accessed something very deep, and it's a glimpse of the depths and or beauty that it provides. Might be a metaphor or something, I don't know. The noise on the artwork seemingly pairs nicely with the tape static present in the reverb of the track too. I like that. And the haziness of the blur seems to represent the kind of distortion that seems to occur at the concluding few minutes of the track.

I think it's being very in the moment, and or emotional, this song, this state. Just being, there.

In the logical side of things, I was listening to my compilation album recently, and I think Down in the Rains of Time made a new impression on me again. I love the depth of it.

I tuned my guitar to that "random" open tuning again too, it just felt like it needed to.

Wait, that reminds me. This was actually on my Ibanez Gio. I don't want to tune my Orville up and down a lot.

I think this song might also be a reflection of how much life means to me, even moreso now. Loss changes you. Time changes you. Or rather, it allows you to realize just how fragile this whole "thing" is. Not in that the world is dangerous all of a sudden, but just in that it really is magical to just be here, with those you love, to see the beautiful sky and plants every day. We are lucky to be here. It is amazing to remember that. Don't ever forget that.

[just posted the song]
..and while working on the artwork, I now remember that I was thinking that the album could maybe be called "Creating Experiences". This is an important thing that I am bringing forward in my life because of the key people that shaped me. I miss them dearly, and I wish I could thank them for our time together one more time. I think that will happen one way or another, somehow.

Edit: one day later, the night.

Listening to this song after having listened to Nonkertompf all the way though, again. Man, that album explains so much without using any words. I don't know if Nonkertompf even has any words or lyrics in it. I love how expressive it is.

The conclusion of the listening of that led me to my song here. I have been wary lately to not compare my songs to other artists, in that sometimes it comes from a place of lack. This time I let myself go to my song though, it felt like it was coming from a place of love, understanding, relation, curiosity, something like that.

What I had gathered while listening to this song, is that it very much seems to come from a place seemingly similar to Nonkertompf, maybe. Again, these are feelings. Usually when I write these feelings out, it tends to make me start to not believe them, because I can see them on the page. Maybe that's something I struggle with.

But, okay. At least in terms of listening habits, this song gathers from a lot of my inspirations. I think it gathers from my recent additions of DTP Ghost, Nonkertompf, and Devin/Keneally in general. The tape degradation feeling/sonic portrayal comes from Steven Wilson's influence. It's not that these things are literal concepts that I am explicitly using with intention. I think it's that it kind of works in parallel, or reciprocally. I seem to gravitate towards music which describes how I feel. I then learn to use those sounds and feelings and paint types in my music. Then it makes it visible as to where I gathered those paint feelings/aesthetics from. So it's not just that it's a composition technique only, it's also the way I felt while listening to the music when I found it. I am re-gathering those feelings again, and using those to paint my music with. So say I felt a certain way while listening to In Absentia for example (I am thinking right now of the intro to Gravity Eyelids for some reason; it's the mellotron that I love). The sound of that, the worbley effect, the emotions I felt from it, or rather how I felt the message it conveys, was perceived by me, that's the thing I am painting with. Not that In Absentia is specific to this song, that's just a relation to this.

While listening to Nonkertompf, I was reading about all of Keneally's work over the years. The more and more I dive into his work, the more I love what he does, how he does it, and am thankful to have someone to look up to like that. It's that he does what he does because it's his story, and he's telling it, and documents it because it's important. In saying that, my own radar says "that sounds like being full of yourself!". My feeling is the total opposite. That's what's so beautiful and inspiring about it. In a way, it reminds me of that thing of when you are a kid, and you have your dreams, and you bring them to fruition. The reasoning of why it is logical or not, we aren't present with yet. I find it beautiful to be able to discern when that logical "no" is unbeneficial, and isn't helping you be happy. In some sense of things, that's why I am loving the music process so much. It's a way for you to become your own advocate, and to do what you do.

I don't want to take the emotion out of this. I tend to explain things very literally. I feel very happy and relatable to so much of his process. It's the safety in feeling the innocence, and to let the process drive the work, rather than some other way.

It's hard to explain how a mental shift affects your life. It's not visible. People might not even perceive that you've changed. But this is what I am trying to articulate. It's unbelievable. I don't know how to explain it to others who don't know what it is. Not like it's some higher-knowledge extravaganza or something (or maybe it is?? lol). It's just that it's only something you can relate to if you've experienced it.

Much also like what this song was rooted in, in an emotional basis, I haven't "understood" loss, until now. I don't know how people experience it, or if it's the same. Of course people handle it differently, but I'm not sure everyone has the same realizations because of it. That in mind, so much of my world has changed because of it too. Let alone the loss of the person or people you love, but the unknown of not having them in your life anymore. It's the finality of it. It's that you grew up and they were always there. You knew they would be gone at some point, not to be blatant or anything. But the realization that they weren't always there either, that's also odd. And realizing that they are just like you, they were young. Not that they were the same them, but young. It's that they had to go through the ropes, just like you. You come to think that they have always known the world. When they are no longer with you, it is shattering. It's not just that they are gone. It's that you realize that they weren't always there. They didn't always know the answers. They taught you everything they learned because you are to do the same. For lack of soul-shattering words, it's beautiful. How this whole "thing" life works, it's amazing. The amount of depth to it is awesome. I'm not even talking about our first-person perception of everyday things, like trees, nature, the world. All of those deserve their own conversations too. Just, the experience of being here, in "now". It's amazing. One recurring thought I keep having is that I am thankful for having been on the same timeline as them. Because that is unfathomably lucky. Luck or not, whatever metric you'd like. The point is that I am so thankful for the time together. It's not even that it's finite. I mean, it is, but the point is that even that was more than the world, you know? This has made everything so good for me, yet also very very very heavy. I already have discerned my time against things I do or don't want to do. But now it means even more now. If I am a bit brash for wanting to stay away from negativity that would only hinder other positive things from coming about, I don't care now. Time is of the essence. We have the ability to decide what we spend our time, our focus, our connections here together. It's not about being "preachy" for good and bad. What does your heart say? Follow it. Put your best foot forward, because that's how you want to be remembered. It's not that you "*should* be remembered nicely". It's that you have the power of so much in front of you. Why get stuck focusing on things that don't matter? Getting mad that someone cut you off in traffic? Silly. Don't waste anymore energy on it. Don't skirt around an uncomfortable conversation because you don't feel like having it. It's just a feeling. It will feel better to go through with it. And the truth is out in the open. It's not doing it for the sake of doing it. It's that you are living by your heart. If people can't handle that, then you don't want them in your life. Make room for those you do care about. Rather than being mad at that other driver, go home and hug your spouse, make them a cake. Take them out to dinner, thank them for the time you have together, and how much they mean the world to you. Those are the moments you want to foster, and to bring forth for you, and for them.

Again, I don't know how to communicate this without being literal. There is a void in where I feel like I don't understand how they can not be here. Is this what existential feelings are all about? I am mourning the times cherished together have now concluded. I am cherishing that what I grew up with is now in the past. I know I am my age, that's not new. But I am realizing how "my age" is now not what it's felt like for the longest time. "Being an adult" is not new, I am a few years into it. Albeit I am still working on independence, making progress! That's surface-level stuff though. On an emotional level, I think I have been young for a long time. Something has changed. I feel it. I know it. I knew "about" the world, but I didn't *understand* it. Now I understand it. And it's soul-rattling. Realizing that people get mad at each other over something they misunderstood. Realizing that people hold grudges because of miscommunication. Realizing that people love each other but don't know how to communicate it. Realizing how much we all need each other. Very much. Realizing how "negative" everyone is. I now see why people say that kids are so happy. Is it because of these realizations about the world we live in? Or is it just another set of misunderstandings which are gained at a certain age? People start to believe that the world is out for them. People think that the world hates them. People think that others hate them. We fuel our own problems, whether cognizant or not. We also fuel our own progress, whether cognizant or not. Kids seems to "work" naturally, making friends, helping before not helping. The environments we grow up in tend to remove this positive light, or rather obstruct it. That's what I am working on and possibly am trying to explain. This light is still there. It's belief in things working out. You may even have factual evidence that things won't work out. But that doesn't mean that you stop trying. That's the whole point. Because what you put in is what you get out, and vice versa. What you don't put in is what you don't get out.

We learn to be okay with getting in our own way, because it's what we're "supposed to do". It's "what everyone else does". It's "being an adult". Fuck it. I won't do that.

title: Can't Quite Quantify
about:
Started a new folder on my iPad, getting back into my "classic inspirations" for how I used to write. I miss it, and I am happy about it again. Even if it's covering familiar ground, I am now seeing that I have a lot to cover there in terms of bringing up the production quality.

So yeah, this was recorded with GarageBand, exactly like the old days. Line out cable from my Line 6 Spider IV (yes), and bass amp sim from GarageBand. Drums tapped out by fingers, my own to be precise. Ibanez Gio.

The change here is that this was then mixed a few days later, and with Logic Pro. I then mastered it, properly, too. I say that because I realized I have been using compressors and limiters wrong, because I didn't realize that they don't activate if the input signal path isn't loud enough. So yeah, makes sense. Just another thing to have learned though, so all good!

Really digging this song! Hear lots of my influences and previous works in it.

Was intending for this to be a full project, and this just would be the first on that. But I think right now might still be a bit taxing with all of the plans I have going on at the moment. I also am just now getting over being sick, this song took a few days longer because of that. Recorded it before I started feeling bad, then had to wait to mix and master it. Finally recouping thankfully.

The big changes in production for this are mainly:
- Flat EQ curve for monitoring while mixing/mastering
- Beyerdynamic DT 990 Pro 250 Ohm (thanks Dad!!)
- Proper compression gain staging
- Direction panning instead of fader panning (they are different!)
- Room volume adjustments (don't just plop reverb on the mix bus, each instrument should have a different amount of reverb on it, accordingly)
- Voxengo Mid Side mastering (ties together both sides of the stereo field)
- Linear Phase EQ for mastering
- Normalization per stem (makes it easier to see unwanted spikes)
- Limiter before Compression and EQ for stems (cut off those spikes just mentioned; not sure if this is good practice, but it does seem to allow the track to behave more consistently)

Not new for this song specifically, but:
- Channel EQ cuts which allow each instrument to breath in it's main EQ slot (thanks Devy!)
- Mixing according to the mix, rather than by buses (I used to "mix" one track at a time, rather than mixing for the whole mix; You mix each track according to how they all work with each other; mindblowing, and makes a lot more sense)
- Compression for each track (specifically as according to what the mix needs as a whole)
- Mastering to LUFS rather than merely -0.1db (While it may still reach -0.1db, the goal is to master to -12 LUFS. I don't know if this is the number that I want specifically for what I need, I have to learn about which apply to what, but so far it seems to sound great. I just don't want to have it anymore where things sound harsh and inconsistent in loudness throughout a track or album. Mastering seems to help with that in general though, even if you don't use LUFS. I think I did for Recreational Outrage though, that was one of the only other projects I did that with. I used it on Izalea recently too, just the other day. That's because I am getting into using it again though. Still have to learn about how applicable it is for what I need. I do want consistent volume levels though, and no piercing high end)
- Adjusting region offsets to account for recording latency (this one is highly significant. So much of my older work was affected by this, heavily. I thought it was my playing that was unable to stay in time [um, it still could be, but that's besides the point 😜], but it's the delay that effects introduce. Or it just might be GB iOS being GB iOS. Idk. It doesn't seem to happen when tracking with Logic on Mac though. I enjoy recording on iPad more though, so this is my solution to it. You can still hear where the timing is a bit weird, that's where I am seemingly accounting for it while in the recording itself. I had used this fix for a few other songs recently, I don't remember which. Any of the newer ones from this fall that I did on my iPad I think I did this offset fix)

So while I could span this out into the start of another album, I am too excited to have this one be complete to wait for the rest of the project to define itself. So, this shall be a single! Maybe I could release this one on it's own too? That could be something surely. Hmm. Thought of this right as I am typing this.

Oh yeah, and to mention GarageBand drums and the bass amp sim, really the sound in the recording was rendered with the Logic Pro equivalents, as that's what I edited and bounced it with. They are the same instruments, yet they tend to sound different between each program, as the Logic Pro ones tend to be higher quality too. For a while, I have enjoyed the novelty of the kind of finicky GarageBand instrument sounds, I kind of like how it plays into the DIY sound of my music. So I have missed that with Logic Pro. But I think I am okay with it actually sounding a little better now. I might have just been getting used to how it sounded, rather than necessarily liking it.

Went crazy on the artwork for this one. This is the second attempt at it. The first one was with a picture I took of some cool clouds and some powerlines. Wasn't feeling inspired. This final one was made from a bunch of post-processing and images from random internet searches. Very similarly composed to how Corruption Junction came out. I like how it conveys the music too. My new technique for making artwork is to listen to the songs the artwork is for while making it. Usually the vibe seems to come across visually more than you realize.
